utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Can the registrar please call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The case number IT-95-17/1-T, the Prosecutor of the Tribunal versus Anto Furundzija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can I have appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Madam President. My name is Patricia Sellers, I am representing the Prosecution, accompanied by my co-counsel, Mr. Mike Blaxill and Ms. Udogaranya.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I name is Luka Misetic. I am Defence Counsel for Mr. Furundzija. I would like to introduce my co-counsel, Mr. Sheldon Davidson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Furundzija, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We have a number of housekeeping matters before we go into closed session as requested by the Prosecution. First of all, let's look at the indictment itself as redacted and amended. I would like to raise a matter with the Prosecution on the indictment regarding paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is it to the intention of the Prosecutor to leave it in?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, are you referring to the predicate paragraph where it says "then Witness A and B, a Bosnian Croat"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no. Your redacted version which reads, paragraph 13 reads: "All acts or omissions set forth herein as grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions of 1949 (grave breaches) and recognised by Article 2 of the Statute of the Tribunal occurred during that armed conflict and partial occupation."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That was to have been withdrawn because that pertained to the counts that the Prosecution would not proceed on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So that is ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, if I might state? We had removed that, and then we were informed later on that the paragraph was to be placed back in, but we are not proceeding under the Geneva Conventions grave breaches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think it was a mistake, a misunderstanding, because we were of the view that you simply showed "redacted," like the other paragraphs are showing, but you leave the numbering in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So it is now understood. It is clear, Mr. Misetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I am not clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Paragraph 13, which reads --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Eighteen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thirteen. One, three. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Which deals with grave breaches of the indictment? The redacted one. The redacted indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I am referring to the amended indictment. Is that what we are referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The one filed on 2nd June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My paragraph 13 does not mention grave breaches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Then we must have a different one. I think you have the original one which had paragraphs --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I can submit it to the court, but this one took out any reference to grave breaches. Perhaps if the court would like to assist me, or the Prosecution, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you give -- yes, the correct version, please, the correct one? That one is supposed to have been withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would the court mind giving me just a minute to read this? I haven't seen this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It is actually -- the original motion with the paragraph that are not required redacted. Otherwise, this is the original form --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The first one which was filed was filed in error, the one with a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe we got the one that was filed in error, but I don't see any problem with it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We move on to the second issue; that is, we would like to know how many witnesses the Prosecution are calling because there seems to have been some changes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and that's one of the reasons that we would like to discuss some of these changes in closed session. What we could inform the court today is we do have witnesses that are ready to proceed. The witness list will, however, change, and we would like to be able to discuss that with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but can't you just tell the Trial Chamber how many witnesses in total.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In open court?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. At this point in time, we will be calling five witnesses. There is a possibility of a sixth. We would like to discuss some of the matters as to the change in our witness composition with the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What about the order?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this, because of the changes, will affect the order, and these are among the things that we would like to discuss with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We will first receive the opening statement of the Prosecution; thereafter, we will go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I just want to ask Defence counsel, anything before the opening statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I guess one of the issues for me is, since I don't know what witnesses are going to be called and not going to be called, that may affect what's in my opening statement, so I guess the Defence would prefer to go to closed session right now so that we can see what exactly we are going to be trying. In addition, we received late Friday afternoon some motions from the Office of the Prosecutor that I think the Defence would prefer be heard first, and then we can proceed with the trial without having to worry about then dealing with motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right then. We will take the order preferred by Defence counsel, that we will go into closed session, deal with everything, iron out everything, before we formally start with an opening statement. We don't need to rise. Is there any need for the court to rise? No. A couple of minutes? Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The court is now in open session, and the oral motion by the Defence on sequestration of witnesses is granted as prayed. We now move forward to asking the Prosecution the order in which they intend to call their witnesses, and since there are so many issues that have come up, maybe you can repeat the approximate timing for evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Good morning, Your Honours, learned counsel. Madam President, Your Honours, the present situation has been described to you as regards the availability of Prosecution witnesses. The order in which we will now propose to call those witnesses to give evidence before this Trial Chamber will commence with a Dr. Muhamed Mujezinovic. Would it be of assistance to the court if I just gave the general parameters of that evidence, the points we are trying to prove?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no. Just the approximate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Just the approximate time. Very well. Dr. Mujezinovic, I do anticipate, would take the better part now, I think, of a day of court hours. If that's, say, a six-hour period or something, I would think that is probably so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That is the evidence in chief only?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That is the evidence in chief. It may be a little bit less, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Approximately six hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I would like to leave that period, Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: As it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Witness B would then follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: E?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: "B" for "Bravo," Ma'am, yes. Madam President, Witness B we anticipate to be able to deliver evidence in chief within a two-hour period; Witness C will follow. Likewise, similar estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Two hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Then we propose Witness D, for "Delta," and we would anticipate probably, I think, four to five hours should cover that evidence, maybe a little less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And then, finally, we have Witness A. Again, we think four to five hours will probably suffice. I may, in fact, have been a little bit over in my estimation in respect of Witness D, but I would prefer to err on the side of caution for the court's planning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blaxill. Defence counsel, anything? The order of witnesses has been given, the estimated time has been given.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Are you prepared to go to trial? The witnesses issue has been sorted out, the order has been given, their identities. Is the Defence prepared to go to trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We are prepared to go to trial, Your Honour, with the caveat as I stated it earlier. Basically we are trying to preserve the issue for appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber doesn't consider that relevant in view of the decisions that have already been given. What we want to know is for you to state unequivocally that you are prepared to go to trial as per the indictment before the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber can adjourn and give the Defence sufficient time as they might need --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't think the Trial Chamber can do that with respect to the issue as we phrased it. We sought relief as to their allegations for the first five elements of Article 7(1) or first five charges under Article 7(1). The motion was denied. So any recess at this point is meaningless because nothing is going to happen during that recess. So what we are saying is, we cannot say we are fully prepared to go to trial on those issues when we have no idea who is going to address those issues, on what basis they have come to the conclusion that Mr. Furundzija ordered somebody to rape Witness A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But, Mr. Misetic, you have the statements of these witnesses, including --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct, and none of them have any allegation whatsoever that Mr. Furundzija ordered anybody to do anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But that is a matter for submission. After the Prosecution have closed their case, that is a matter for submission, in which case you can tailor your defence accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I think I have stated it for the record. I don't know why they have brought the charge then if there is no witness who is going to address the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Isn't that for submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct. But if something should come out at trial where they start to call a witness who is going to say, "I heard Mr. Furundzija order Mr. X" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. Mr. Misetic, these are the witnesses lined up and the statements have been given --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We are prepared to go forward, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we can proceed to the opening statement. We are supposed to adjourn at 12.30 because we are sharing the services with the other Chamber, so do you think we would finish by 12.30?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I think my friend has an observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Misetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: With respect to that, that's fine with the Defence. I wondered, just as a technical matter, if we start questioning witnesses with respect to Witness A, let's say, technically how do we go about doing that, let's say, with Dr. Mujezinovic, who is in open session? Are we to assume he has full knowledge as to identities of witnesses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- that he knows who Witness A is or the name the pseudonym covers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You can't bring that up in open session because then it will vitiate our order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right. So how do I question? Do you want me to go into closed session when we start talking about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. You can question a witness in open session by putting the evidence or whatever statement you have or other allegations without necessarily identifying the witness. That is possible. "There is an allegation to this aspect. What did you say to that?" You put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I say, "Do you know Witness B?" And he says, "I have no idea what Witness B means ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe I can ask the Prosecution. Maybe they can assist.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I understand correctly, I think Defence counsel is wondering, can he say the names of other witnesses out during an open session in his cross-examination? I would suggest, and I think if this issue does come up, from the Prosecution's point of view, for example, if we have to refer to another witness, we would then ask the court, "Could we please go into closed session?" We would take all precautionary measures and certainly insist that Defence counsel not mention the names of pseudonym witnesses. I believe that is his concern. Other than that, if he would like to know the identity of witnesses in terms of purposes for cross-examination or for direct examination and, therefore, we would be in the opposite situation, I imagine that there is a manner in which the witness's name can be shown to the person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: On a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- and not mention that name, and then we can proceed. I believe that is his concern that he has put forward to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is exactly it, Your Honour. I just was wondering whether the witness would get a sheet of paper or something that says "Witness A equals X, Witness D equals Y," et cetera. That was my only concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. That is settled. So we will go ahead with the opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Madam President, Your Honours. The case before you, unlike any other that has come before this Tribunal to date, focuses essentially on one horrific day in the life of one civilian woman, and it is upon the facts of that day that you will be invited to convict the accused upon the counts that are indicted. The counts before you alleged against the accused are torture and outrages upon personal dignity, including rape. The allegations embrace offences which the Statute of the Tribunal and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence have specifically addressed by incorporating provisions for victims of sexual assaults and rape in war, subsequent to the concerns that were expressed by the United Nations Secretary-General in the report of the 3rd of May, 1993. This Honourable Trial Chamber, Your Honours, is now charged with trying these two counts of serious violations of international humanitarian law which are charged under Article 3 of the Statute of the International Tribunal. The mandate of the International Tribunal does include the most culpable and also the most notorious war crimes during the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, and the experiences of the victim in this case are, indeed, notorious. The case before Your Honours is focused upon the events of one day, the 15th of May, 1993, and they involve what happened to one female civilian taken from her home by members of a military unit of the forces known as the HVO, or the Croatian Defence Council, armed forces in the area in Central Bosnia which had become known as the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. This unit was called the Jokers, and they took her to their headquarters building where she was interrogated. The evidence will show the accused was a member of that unit and that it was he who conducted the interrogation along with another member of his unit. Shortly after the interrogation started, the other member of the Jokers forced the victim, Witness A, to undress, and then began what turned out to be a prolonged series of physical, mental, and serious sexual abuses, including repeated rapes. The evidence, Your Honours, will show that the accused conducted that interrogation and, after a while, arranged a confrontation with another detainee during which both were beaten, and the female victim was again subjected to further horrendous sexual abuse in the presence of her interrogator. You will, in fact, hear that it was about 10.30 hours on the morning of that day that the members of the Jokers, as I say, a well-known special unit of the HVO in the area around Vitez in Central Bosnia, took her to that headquarters in a hamlet called Nadioci a short distance from Vitez. Your Honours, I would at this time interrupt this part of my address and make reference to a visual aid that I have provided to the assistance of the court and the Defence. There is a map you will see on the easel present in the courtroom, it is a published document, and it simply shows the area of Vitez and surrounds. For Your Honours' assistance, however, just geographically to place the events, I have had copies prepared because this is not a very good visual exhibit from a distance. Those copies are available to you, and I have supplied them to the Defence, together with a schematic just showing the location of the Vitez area within Bosnia and in relation to two of the major towns in the area Zenica and the capital city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have them numbered before they are distributed?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, when you have an opportunity to see that, you will see thereon that marked in green is the town of Vitez; marked in pink, to the other end of the geographical area known as the Lasva Valley, is the town of Busovaca; and in between the two, just north of the main road running out of Vitez, edged in green and pink, the small village or hamlet of Nadioci. It is in that general geographic area that the events of this day took place in the building in Nadioci and that the armed conflict took place during those months. Your Honours, the headquarters building was a small restaurant known locally as "the Bungalow," adjacent to which were a number of small summerhouses which were used by the Jokers as their barrack accommodation. When the victim, Witness A, arrived at the Bungalow, she was placed in that barrack accommodation of the Joker soldiers, a number of whom were present. She heard words that they were "waiting for the boss," and a short time later, she then heard soldiers saying, "Furundzija is here." She says a man appeared in the room, and she concluded from the arrival of that man that he was the Furundzija whose name she had heard. Her evidence will show that the accused held a piece of paper and uttered the words to the effect that he had an indictment for her, or something of that order, and then proceeded to interrogate her about a list of Croatian names that she may know or have contact with. He asked about her sons and whether they were in the Bosnian army and a number of other matters. Witness A will say that she answered she did not know the names that he stated. Apparently this appeared not to be to the liking of the accused, who responded that she would soon answer. Then the evidence will show she was suddenly seized by the hair, and another member of the Jokers unit, who told her his nickname was Cicko, said she would soon "know him." At that point, this man, Cicko, demanded that Witness A undress. She did so to the point of complete nudity and then said that this man began to stroke her naked body with a knife and threatened to insert it into her vagina if she did not tell the truth, and then, after that, commenced raping her by both vaginal and oral penetration. During this, Your Honours, the accused is alleged to have persisted with his interrogation questions. He did not stop questioning her whilst this was happening. And, indeed, this took place in the presence of the group of Jokers soldiers. Witness A will say that it seemed to her that after each unsatisfactory response by her to the questions put by the accused, more sexual abuse was inflicted upon her by the man known as Cicko. After some time, Witness A will say the accused became angry at her obviously unsatisfactory responses and told her he would confront her with someone else. The next thing she knew is that the accused and other soldiers had left the room and she found herself alone with this man, Cicko. She suffered further rapes and abuse at his hands before another soldier came in, gave her a blanket, and took her to another room, a smaller one she described as a pantry. The man, Cicko, followed. In that room, there was the encounter with the person who is referred to in the indictment as Victim B and who, in these proceedings, will be Witness D, and that person was brought in by the accused, Anto Furundzija. Victim B, or I should say now Witness D, appeared severely bruised about the face, and it was quite clear to Witness A that he had been badly beaten. The man was dressed in the uniform of an HVO military policeman. Witness A will then say that the accused, Furundzija, said words to the effect, "Now we'll see who is telling the truth." So now we have a continuation, a second phase to the interrogation process, in which both the accused and his fellow Joker, Cicko, have been participants to date and continue to be. Both the victims were then beaten, particularly across the feet, with a pair of batons wielded by Cicko and another member of the unit, police batons. Witness A then recalls Cicko using words to the effect not to hit her as he had "other methods for a woman." Cicko is then alleged to have started raping her again. On this occasion, vaginal penetration, anal penetration, and oral penetration. Witness A felt that she recalled some further questions about her sons from the accused in the course of these events in the pantry. So in that small room, Your Honours, we have Witness A beaten and raped while being observed by the accused, and Witness A will say that other Jokers were standing by the open door of this pantry watching what transpired. Eventually, it ended, and the traumatised lady was taken by another Joker soldier to the original barrack room and allowed eventually to dress. Your Honours, these are the essential facts that you will hear, and these are the facts upon which Your Honours are charged to judge the guilt or otherwise of the accused in respect of the counts of torture and outrages upon personal dignity, including rape. Whilst Rule 96 does not require corroboration of the testimony of a rape victim, the Prosecution does propose to call, of course, Witness D, who will be able to corroborate at least a part of the appalling abuses that were suffered by Witness A that day. Furthermore, the link of the crimes to the armed conflict will, the Prosecution submits, be shown by the fact that this was in the context of a prolonged interrogation seeking information about matters of relevance to the accused in the performance of a duty that day. He was at work. Before submitting the victim testimony of Witness A and Witness D, the Prosecution will be bringing evidence to establish the circumstances and events which led to the armed conflict in the region. We must necessarily cover, not in extenso, but the political divisions, the ethnic tensions, and eventual outbreaks of violence that led to the descent into armed conflict within the region. Your Honours, we propose to adduce this evidence essentially through our witnesses de fact, our civilian witnesses who were involved in the events in their own region and therefore can speak to the actual manifestations of the existence of an armed conflict. One such witness, the first you will hear, is a medical doctor who became drawn into public affairs in the community and dealings between the ethnic and political entities in the area before and during the armed conflicts. This witness can also speak to the physical manifestations of the conflict for the civilians in the area and also the fact that he treated, as a doctor, the wounded of all sides, military and civilian persons, in a war hospital, and this being one such manifestation of the existence of armed conflict and its duration within the area of Vitez. Other witnesses will also speak to the existence of armed conflict but will, in turn, identify the accused, the Jokers unit, and their headquarters, as forming part of a competent entity; in other words, official uniformed participants under arms in the armed conflict. Accordingly, Your Honours, the accused was governed by the laws and customs of war, just as Witness A is, and certainly should have been then, a beneficiary of their protection. As stated by the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic case, Your Honours, when discussing armed conflict and the parameters for the application of international humanitarian law to armed conflict, it was stated: "An armed conflict exists whenever there is a resort to armed force between states or protracted armed violence between governmental authorities and organised armed groups or between such groups within a state," and that the international law application is that "International humanitarian law applies from the initiation of such armed conflicts and extends beyond the cessation of hostilities until a general conclusion of peace is reached or, in the case of internal conflicts, peaceful settlement is achieved ... The law continues to apply throughout the territory of a warring state or the entire territory controlled by a party to an internal conflict." Your Honours, the evidence will show that a state of armed conflict was ongoing in the region where these crimes were committed. Madam President, Your Honours, I will now tend to the theory of criminal responsibility advanced by the Prosecution in this case. The counts against the accused allege criminal responsibility for his participation in these crimes under Article 7(1) of the Statute of the International Tribunal. The Prosecution submits, as we have set forth in the Prosecutor's reply regarding the application of the Article that has been filed with this Chamber, that the Article contains a number of independent provisions which give rise to criminal responsibility, individually or in combination. Firstly, under Article 7(1), a person who planned, instigated, ordered, committed a crime bears individual responsibility. We say that by conducting an interrogation under the circumstances described by Witness A, by transferring the victim to another room, by bringing in the other person for the confrontation, and remaining while further beating and sexual abuse occurred, marks the accused as a direct perpetrator committing the crimes of torture and outrages upon personal dignity, including rape. You may feel that when you have heard all of the evidence that others of the limbs of the article, such as instigation, may be made out, but it is the Prosecution case that these are independent individual limbs and any one may be applied to establish criminal responsibility. It is our respectful submission that it is open to you, as Judges of the Trial Chamber, to assess that, as to whether one or more will apply at the end of the evidence. That article, 7(1), also includes persons who aided and abetted in the planning, preparation, or execution of a crime referred to in Articles 2 to 5 of the Statute, and they also shall bear individual criminal responsibility. Again, the Prosecution submits that these are individual but, at the same time, complementary limbs of responsibility, and you may find one or more of them fulfilled upon the evidence. The Tribunal already has some jurisprudence on the question of aiding and abetting, and this has been set out in the Prosecution Pre-Trial brief filed on the 22nd of May. Here, however, the Prosecutor submits that the accused, by conducting the interrogation of Witness A and the confrontation with Witness B, remaining present without any word or deed or, at the very least, disapproval, lent sufficient support and encouragement to his comrade who was committing the acts of rape, and the Prosecution submits that the facts will show that it constituted aiding and abetting in the rape. Your Honours, I will now deal briefly with the elements of the specific charges and the application of Article 3 of the Statute of the Tribunal in determining the scope of the laws and customs of war as the Prosecution will submit. I will quote, if I may, from the Appeals Chamber decision in the case of Tadic, stating that: "Article 3 is a general clause covering all violations of humanitarian law not falling under Article 2 or covered by Articles 4 and 5, more specifically: (i) violations of The Hague law of international conflicts; (ii) infringements of provisions of the Geneva Conventions other than those classified as 'grave breaches' ... (iii) violations of Common Article 3 and other customary rules of internal conflicts; (vi) violations of agreements binding upon the parties to the conflict, considered qua treaty law, i.e., agreements which have not turned into customary international law." It was then stated that: "Article 3 functions as a residual clause designed to ensure that no serious violation of international humanitarian law is taken away from the jurisdiction of the International Tribunal." The Appeals Chamber also specified jurisdictional prerequisites which must be met for an offence to be subject to prosecution under Article 3 of the Statute, and those are likely discussed in the Pre-Trial brief already filed with Your Honours. The Prosecution submits that the evidence I have already outlined should meet those very conditions. Moreover, the Appeals Chamber also concluded that so long as these conditions are met, it does not matter whether the "serious" violation occurred within the context of an international or an internal armed conflict. Hence, Your Honours, the intention of the Prosecution to fulfil its obligation by showing the existence of the armed conflict without extensive evidence or any, indeed, specifically directed to its classification. The Appeals Chamber in its decision on jurisdiction in the Tadic case also addressed the nexus between crimes and conflict which, if I may paraphrase: " ... placed a broad geographic and temporal frame to apply the protection to the beneficiaries of Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions outside the narrow geographical context of the actual theatre of combat operations." The Appeals Chamber stated that the nexus required is only this: That there is "a relationship between the conflict and the (acts), not that the acts occurred in the midst of battle." In the present case, the accused is charged under Article 3 with violations of Common Article 3 to the Geneva Conventions and of Article 4(2)(e) of Additional Protocol II to those Conventions. The Appeals Chamber has held that "customary international law imposes criminal liability for serious violations of Common Article 3, as supplemented by other general principles and rules on the protection of victims of internal armed conflict, and for breaches of certain fundamental principles and rules regarding means and methods of combat in civil strife." The Prosecutor interprets those fundamental guarantees protected by Article 4 of Additional Protocol II as supplementing Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions. To apply Common Article 3, there are certain requirements to be fulfilled: "(a) The unlawful acts were committed in the context of an armed conflict." And here we say a civilian falling into the hands of a party to that conflict. "(b) The perpetrator was connected to one side involved in the conflict." Indeed so. A serving member of one of the combatant parties. "(c) The victims were persons taking no active part in hostilities, which includes civilians --" Witness A was. "-- members of the armed forces even who laid down their arms or otherwise rendered hors de combat by sickness, wounds, detention or any other cause." And finally, "(d) One of the enumerated acts listed in Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions were committed." And that is contained in the indictment. The Prosecution submits that the evidence outlined above satisfies those conditions. Now, Your Honours, with your leave, I will differentiate briefly between the two counts. The Prosecutor has already set forth in the Pre-Trial brief definitions of torture and outrages upon personal dignity. As for the torture count, the evidence will show, what? Firstly, the accused must, by acts or omissions, intentionally inflict severe physical or mental pain or suffering upon the victim for one or a combination of any of the following purposes. That is the point, Your Honours: by acts or omissions, intentionally inflicts severe physical or mental pain or suffering upon the victim. What purposes apply? The first, to obtain information or a confession from that person or a third person. This was an interrogation. Secondly, to punish the victim or a third person for an act committed or suspected of having been committed by either of them. Thirdly, for the purpose of intimidating or coercing the victim or a third person. At that point, we have the second phase of the interrogation, Witness A and the other party, Witness D, in the confrontational position. Is that intimidating, coercion? And then, finally, for any reason based upon discrimination of any kind. You must then show that the accused was himself an official or acted at the instigation of or with the consent or acquiescence of an official or person acting in an official capacity. Your Honours, this was a uniformed soldier on duty. The offence of torture is complete when severe pain or suffering is inflicted and does not require that serious injury to body or health result. I feel confident the facts that you hear from Witness A will satisfy any possible definition of severe pain or suffering. So, Your Honours, the evidence here is this: We have a serving military official who interrogates a civilian, seeking information and admissions from her, intimidating her, trying to coerce her responses to his satisfaction. The facts you hear from Witness A, as I say, will bear out the criteria of the count of torture. With regard to the outrages on personal dignity, the definitions are brief, but they encompass acts which denigrate, humiliate, or attack personal integrity, including the sexual integrity of the victim. In Common Article 3(1)(c), outrages upon dignity include conduct which is considered, in particular, humiliating or degrading. Again, Your Honours, I refer to the very core of this case, Witness A, and the horrendous experience that she recounts having endured at the hands of the accused and his Joker comrades, held naked before the accused, interrogated by him, interrogated as threatened by this man, Cicko, then subjected to forced sexual acts of vaginal rape and oral rape in the presence of other military comrades, again further beaten and raped within the room when confronted with Victim B, Witness D as he will be, again with the accused present as the official interrogator, seemingly content for all this to happen and to happen openly in front of other members of their unit. We suggest that even if there had been no more than the interrogation of a lady in a state of forced nudity, this offence of outrages would be made out, but in this case, Your Honours, as you have heard and will hear, much more happened. As I've indicated, Madam President, Your Honours, this case depends on few witnesses but they are noble people who are prepared to come here, not for the first time, and they are going to subject themselves to reliving these events but they are going to serve the international community in the cause of justice for the victims of war crimes. The case is not the property of the Prosecution, nor the property of the Defence but, indeed, is the faith of these people who are looking to Your Honours to be the arbiters of the truth. That is my opening address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. We have some 20 minutes before we adjourn for this afternoon, but I think it would be better to start calling witnesses in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, to remind you, the Defence does have an opening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Not at this stage because we were of the view that the Defence would address the court in their opening statement before they start the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe under the rules we are entitled to open right now, and we would like to open right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Of course. You can go ahead. Yes, Mr. Misetic, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I said, yes, Mr. Misetic, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May it please the court, again, my name is Luka Misetic, along with my co-counsel, Sheldon Davidson, we will be defending Mr. Furundzija in this trial. The Prosecution will try hard to convince you that should convict Anto Furundzija. They will spin tales unrelated to the 15th of May, 1993 in an attempt to bias this court and divert attention from the facts and issues that are before this Trial Chamber. But no matter how hard they try, they cannot get around one simple fact: Anto Furundzija was not present for any sexual assault on Witness A. The Prosecution in this case has charged Anto Furundzija with interrogating a woman while she was being sexually assaulted and beaten on the feet with a baton. The evidence in this case will show you that Anto Furundzija is not guilty of these charges. Witness D will tell you that, contrary to the allegations in paragraphs 25 and 26 of the amended indictment, Anto Furundzija was not present for any sexual assault on Witness A. Part of your duties in this case will be to determine whether the testimony of Witness A is so reliable that her testimony, and her testimony alone, convinces you beyond a reasonable doubt that Anto Furundzija is guilty as charged. And make no mistake, the Prosecution's entire case is based on her testimony. The first few witnesses have no firsthand knowledge relevant to the allegations contained in the amended indictment. The fourth witness, Witness D, will directly contradict Witness A as to crucial allegations against Mr. Furundzija that are contained in the indictment. The Prosecution's case, therefore, is a one-witness case, and you must believe that one witness. You will hear testimony from Witness A who, on direct examination by the Prosecution, will appear sincere and she will appear confident. You, like everyone else in the courtroom, will sympathise with this woman because of what she has endured. Confidence, however, is not a barometer of reliability. The evidence will show you that Witness A is wrong, not that she is a liar, but that she is wrong, that the circumstances of the crime and the difficulties of the identification process make it impossible to share her opinion as it relates to Mr. Furundzija beyond a reasonable doubt. There is already reasonable doubt in this case. Mr. Blaxill's opening statement varies greatly from the allegations in the indictment and the 1995 statement upon which the indictment is based. You will have the opportunity at the close of the evidence to compare the 1995 statement, the indictment and its allegations, and the opening statement by Mr. Blaxill. Witness A will take the stand. She will be a sympathetic witness. Every one of us will wish we could undo her trauma and compensate her somehow for her ordeal. She will come before you and she will tell you a story, a story that she has been asked repeatedly over the last five years to develop, to revise and to repeat. Trying to recollect the events of 1993, her mind has come to accept as true her reconstruction of events in May, June and July of 1993. It is that reconstruction of events that you will hear in this courtroom. We believe that the evidence will show that her reconstruction is inaccurate and unreliable. It is solely upon her reconstruction of events that the indictment in this case is based. We believe that Witness A's lack of reliability will require you to acquit Mr. Furundzija at the close of the Prosecution's case. Witness A will testify that in 1995 she told the Prosecution's investigators that on the morning of the 15th of May, 1993, she was taken by three members of the Jokers from her apartment in Vitez to a weekend house near a bungalow in Nadioci, Bosnia. Upon arrival, according to her 1995 statement, she is asked questions about certain individuals about whom she knows nothing. She claims in her 1995 statement that she is then grabbed from behind by Bralo who puts a knife to her throat and threatens her. He then proceeds to sexually assault Witness A outside the presence of Mr. Furundzija. You will find that in the 1995 statement. You will find that in the indictment itself in this case. After Bralo had perpetrated these acts, Witness A claimed in 1995 that Anto Furundzija then entered the room. She alleges that this man she identifies as Anto Furundzija asked her some questions, at least she did say that in 1995. She alleges that while this man was asking her questions, Bralo took a knife and placed it along her leg and threatened her. He did not cut her, stab her or strike her in any way. Witness A, in 1995, did not allege that she was beaten or assaulted by anyone in this room while the person she claims to be Anto Furundzija was present. At most, Witness A in 1995 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down for the benefit of the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, can you slow down for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, yes. At most, Witness A will testify that she was exposed to questioning combined with a verbal threat. That's according to her 1995 statement. She will tell you on cross-examination that she was taken to another room which, in one statement she referred to as the pantry, by Bralo, the man she alleges to be Mr. Furundzija, and a third man. She then claims that Witness D was ushered into this pantry and that all of the other soldiers were in the hallway. That is the way paragraph 26 of the indictment reads. What happened in those few minutes in the pantry is what is really in dispute here, and you must decide whether Witness A convinces you beyond a reasonable doubt that you should resolve that dispute by convicting Anto Furundzija. Witness A will testify that in that room she and Witness D were both beaten by Bralo and that she was, again, sexually assaulted by Bralo also in the presence of Witness D. Anto Furundzija, she will tell you, was present interrogating both her and Witness D. It is upon that testimony that the Prosecution indicted Mr. Furundzija and the indictment was confirmed. But you will see that the Prosecution has now disavowed that 1995 statement because Witness A gave materially different evidence in a different case before this Tribunal. The evidence will show you that even this new theory collapsed two weeks ago. They located Witness D and took his statement, and Witness D stated, "Witness A is simply wrong." Witness D, the Prosecution's own witness, will tell that you the allegations against Mr. Furundzija in paragraph 26 of the amended indictment are wrong. Witness D told the Prosecutors, "I know for sure that during the time that Witness A and I were in the room in the summerhouse and Witness A was sexually mistreated by Bralo, Anto Furundzija was not present in the same room." Witness D thus directly contradicts Witness A's recollection of events. That, in and of itself, raises a reasonable doubt. The Prosecution in their case in chief will desperately try to downplay the significance of that statement. The Prosecution will claim that Witness D does not exculpate Anto Furundzija, but the Prosecution even admitted as such by producing the statement, at least partially, pursuant to Rule 68. Despite the Prosecution's efforts, you will, at the very least, find that Witness D's testimony creates a reasonable doubt about the guilt of Anto Furundzija. Witness A was exchanged, according to her, on August 15th, 1993. She arrived in the town of Zenica. She will tell you that she only saw the man she claims as Anto Furundzija for a few minutes on the 15th of May, 1993. She had never seen him before; she has never seen him after. You will find that Witness A's testimony, through no fault of her known, is not credible, let alone convincing beyond a reasonable doubt. We expect the evidence to show that Witness A, as with others who have been subjected to such experiences, did what she could when she arrived in Zenica to suppress those memories and move on with her life. But then the investigators entered her life. She was now forced to retrieve from her memory whatever she could from those traumatic days. You will hear how her recollection changes from statement to statement. The Defence will show you why her statements change from day to day, from month to month, from year to year. All of us will remember this trial for many years, and when we retell it to our friends and family, we will remember the Prosecution's witnesses. We will probably not remember their names or whether they comprised three men and two women or four women and one man. We will probably not remember the names of the Prosecutors or the Defence counsel. What we will remember is the event and the general nature of the charges and our impressions. People in Witness A's situation make mistakes in memory. The evidence will show that memory is not a camera that takes a photograph of certain events. Stress does not sharpen our memory; in fact, it dulls it. And the length of time involved, five years from the date of the occurrence, also weakens our image of the past. Memory, the evidence will show, is actually an opinion or a belief as to what occurred. The Prosecution's entire case is built on Witness A's ability, not just to recollect general events, but specific facts such as who entered a room at what time or what event happened in which order. The evidence will show you, Your Honours, that Witness A's memory is not reliable and that the Prosecution cannot meet its burden of proof. Your Honours, at the close of the Prosecution's case in chief, you too will have come to the same conclusion. I'm confident that, at the conclusion of the Prosecutor's case, you will not be able to find evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Furundzija committed these crimes. The lack of evidence in this case will compel this Chamber to return a verdict of not guilty. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, would you help us with this? There's going to be evidence about the existence of an armed conflict at the material time. Is it disputed that there was an armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It may be, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think at this juncture we will adjourn and start the case with the witnesses in the afternoon, but I would like to give an overview of the schedules. This case is scheduled for this week and next week. Our sittings in the mornings start at 9.30 to 12.30; in the afternoon 14.00 to 17.00. On Friday, we will shall only up to 11.00, we have another function regarding another courtroom, and then in the afternoon we have proceedings in another case. So on Friday, we shall adjourn at 11.00 hours. The trial will resume on Monday at 09.30 and continue the hours up to Thursday. We shall not sit on Friday next week. We are hoping that the Prosecution's case will be completed by then. Any other matters before we rise?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I raise one point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, just about the motion you granted in terms of sequestration, would you agree that as the Prosecution has spoken to its witness today, that we meet that sequestration requirement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: As the Prosecution has done what?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has already spoken to its witnesses concerning the concerns that were raised by learned counsel that we meet your sequestration requirements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the Trial Chamber has already granted the motion actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The court will rise and resume at 14.00 sharp. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.26 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-17/1, the Prosecutor of the Tribunal versus Anto Furundzija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The accused, can you hear me in the language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it appearances are as before. The witness, please make your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Yes, the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Madam President, Your Honours, thank you. Yes, I call now the first Prosecution witness, Dr. Muhamed Mujezinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Doctor. Do you hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, would you please give your full name to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm Dr. Muhamed Mujezinovic, son of Adem, born at the village of Horvina, the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You've given the title of doctor. What is your exact profession, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a physician, an internal medicine specialist and a specialist for occupational medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When did you, in fact, train and qualify as a medical practitioner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I graduated from the faculty in Sarajevo in 1978. Then I underwent specialisation in internal medicine in 1984 and occupational medicine in 1989 and post-graduate studies in assessment of the work ability, and I was educated in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Where have you performed the majority of your professional life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My first job as a physician was in Doboj. And then a year and a half later, I was invited by the then authorities in Vitez to move to Vitez where I was born and where I completed my primary education. In Vitez, I was a general practitioner since 1st September, 1979. Until occasions, I was also the head of the medical centre in Vitez, the first time in 1980, and then for two months I was as director in October and November '92.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a moment, Doctor? Did you have any other roles in your medical work for the health authorities? Did you do any voluntary work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As a physician, I worked for sports clubs in Vitez as a volunteer, completely free, that is, I had all the sportsmen, all the athletes in Vitez under my charge. I worked as a -- this was a kind of humanitarian activity in my leisure time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, would you describe briefly what kind of community Vitez was and what ethnic groups lived in Vitez prior, say, to 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vitez is a small industrial town, a sports town too. The municipality of Vitez had a population of some 28,000 of different ethnic origin. The majority, I think, were Croats, something around 12,000; then Muslims, slightly over 11,000; and I guess some 5,000 Serbs, and some others too. So it was an ethnically mixed community in Vitez; all together, about 28,000 inhabitants. Some 8,600 of them were full-time employed working either in Vitez or adjacent places, that is, Zenica and Travnik, but also the inhabitants of Zenica and Travnik held jobs in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What, up to the year of 1990, were the general relations between ethnic groups within that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that area, the inter-ethnic relations were very good. I cannot remember -- ever since I got my job in Vitez on the 1st of September in '79 -- I cannot remember a single inter-ethnic conflict. I often cooperated with the local police. When they would do investigations citing cases of traffic accidents and other accidents that would take place in the municipality of Vitez territory, I cannot remember a single inter-ethnic incident at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, in the year of 1990, did any specific political parties emerge in the Vitez area or in Bosnia generally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Across Bosnia and in Vitez too, new parties emerged. They were called national parties. Croats set up their HDZ, the Croat Democratic Alliance; the Muslims, the Party for Democratic Action; and the Serbs, the Serb Democratic Party. In other words, they were all founded in 1990 or, perhaps, a little earlier. I cannot remember exactly but, at any rate, those three national parties were founded at that time by people who lived in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did those parties openly represent the interests of the specific ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The programmes of all these parties which, as I have said, were all national, they promoted the interests of individual ethnic communities, that is, Muslims, Croats and Serbs in our area, in our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could you tell me, please, who became the leaders of the HDZ, the Croat party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I recollect properly, the first HDZ president in Vitez was Mr. Anto Valenta; the first SDA president was Hajrudin Karic; and the SDS was headed by Jovica Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were elections held in the month of November 1990 in your region and nationally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The elections took place in November 1990 and that included our municipality. These elections were won by national parties, that is, HDZ. They ranked the first in terms of the number of notes; then SDA ranked second. The SDS, as there were very few Serbs there, had only two votes. And other parties which participated in the elections won a certain number of votes, that is, a certain number of seats in the local assembly. For instance, LC, that is, League of Communists, the Party for Democratic Change, eight; the democratic party, three; HDZ, 23; SDA, 16; the Socialist Alliance of Democratic Youth, two seats; and the Democratic Alliance of Socialists won one seat in the Vitez assembly, municipal hall. The municipality assembly, that is, had some 60 delegates who were to represent the local population in the hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That, essentially, was the local governing body, was it, the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was the local parliament. We called it the assembly of the municipality. It was the highest authority in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you have any political involvement in the community at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a member of SDA but I was not actively involved. I became an SDA member in August 1990. I was an observer at all public rallies and fora organised by individual parties in our place, in our locality, and I listened to the presentations by representatives of the neutral parties, that is, their programmes, their programme objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, did you take any active part in local politics after that date, after 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In September '91, I became the first vice-president of the executive committee of Vitez SDA. At that time, I became actively involved in the Party for Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I believe you said that the SDA was the party that represented the interests of the Muslim population at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, largely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What was the relationship of the executive board of the party to the governmental assembly, the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, the relations were quite good. Yes, at the time, they were quite good. I'm referring to September '91.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What did the executive board do in terms of its powers within the community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The executive board of the SDA, of the Party for Democratic Action, would get a list of questions of topics to be addressed by the assembly; that is, we were supposed to take a stand or to take a position on individual issues in Vitez, and the board suggested, proposed to our delegates to represent, to advocate the views proposed at the meetings of the executive board. It was not binding on them but it was advisable.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: In the course of your duties on the executive board, did you have dealings with your counterparts in the other parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is a small place. We regularly met and I had a public job in Vitez. I knew most of its inhabitants, the Vitez inhabitants, and I also met councilmen who represented us on the assembly of all nationalities, that is, of all ethnic origin; that is, I simply cooperated with them by the nature of my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Who was the president of the municipal assembly at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We say that at the first democratic elections as reported in Vitez, a representative of HDZ, Mr. Ivan Santic was elected. He is an applied chemist.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Is Mr. Santic a -- [Note: Balance of question obliterated by answer following].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An applied chemist. Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, taking you forward towards the end of 1991, were relations between the ethnic communities and their political representatives still harmonious?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Throughout '91, there were no, or at least I do not know of any, noteworthy problems when it comes to these relations. As far as I know, they were in some common discussions, each one advocating his own attitude. And, in the end, a vote would be cast on any problem, that is, on any issue raised in the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, when, in the course of events in Vitez, did you first hear the expression or name "Herceg-Bosna"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time I heard this term "Herceg-Bosna" from our delegate at the meeting of the executive board of SDA, that the president of the municipal assembly, Ivan Santic, had notified the delegates that the community of Herceg-Bosna had just been established. This was in late 1991. And then he stated that this cultural community of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina would not threaten the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, other peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Subsequent to that, if I can move to March of 1992, what was the position of the municipal assembly in March of '92?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In March '92, if I remember, we held our assembly of all the councilmen elected to our municipal assembly, and the Croat Democratic Union, the HDZ, had suggested to set up the crisis committee of the municipality of Vitez which would take over the powers and the authority of the municipal assembly and the executive board of the municipal assembly. The last session of the assembly was, therefore, held in March, and the SDA delegates, they were asked what was that, the Croat community Herceg-Bosna, and the delegates of SDP, Navinka Rajic, asked whether it was true that the Croats in Vitez were receiving arms. And a representative of HDZ, who is also the police chief in Vitez, Pero Skopljak, and Ivan Santic denied this. Ivan Santic said that the Croat community of Herceg-Bosna, he repeated it was a cultural community of Croats, that it would not pose a threat to the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina and other peoples living in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What were these circumstances, Doctor, that prompted the suggestion for a crisis staff? What was happening in Vitez that prompted people to want to suggest this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina and, therefore, in Vitez too, we had very many problems, first with refugees arriving from east Croatia, then from east and west Bosnia. And since the assembly is a large body, that is, comprising 60 councilmen represent -- the HDZ members suggested an operative body which could meet more easily and take decisions more easily. And one of our representatives, Mila Frompa, who was a lawyer and a member of the executive board of the HDZ, said that it was not in line with the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that we should set up the wartime presidency of Vitez. And this was accepted just for the sake of peace in the House, but it was said that it needed to be verified by the municipal assembly of the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that the crisis staff was, in fact, formed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And what was its composition, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The crisis staff was based on a parity basis, five Muslims, five Croats. It was chaired by Ivan Santic, that is, the president of the municipal assembly; Fuad Kaknjo, he was the vice-president of the government; then Pero Skopljak, who was the chief of the police; Josip Celic and Vlado Santic. The Muslim side was represented by the SDA president in Vitez, Mujip Kajic, Fuad Kaknjo. I was made responsible for the medical side and Sulejman Kasagic, and the commander of the Territorial Defence, Hakija Cengic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So in the face of these refugees, were you aware of the causes of those refugees coming to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we knew that while there was war in Croatia, as far as I know, some three Croats and one Muslim left to that war as volunteers. When the war spread to Bosnia, then every evening we could see it on television or hear on the radio that their combat operations in east Bosnia and west Bosnia, and from those areas refugees were arriving in Vitez. The majority of them came from Knetiza near Foca, then from Kozarac, from Kljuc, Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you make any medical preparations to receive people and treat people in these circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In Vitez, we had already had our Red Cross organisation and all the refugees were put on record with the Red Cross. Prior to that, humanitarian societies were set up. The Croats founded Caritas, and the Muslims set up Merhamet. So we took care of accommodating those people, by and large, in summer cottages or those people who had large houses and therefore could accommodate them. In Vitez, as I was also the vice-president of Merhamet, there were over 4,000 refugees, Muslim refugees, in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, during this time, you were serving on the crisis staff, how often did that staff meet to deal with administrative and governmental issues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The crisis staff would meet very often, almost on a daily basis, sometimes even two times a day if necessary. This depended, of course, on the problems that were on the agenda at that time. It was Mr. Ivan Santic who would convene the meeting of the crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Would it be true to say that the crisis staff had effectively become the main authority in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And what were the relations between essentially the Croat element of the crisis staff and the Muslim element of the crisis staff? What were their relations in handling these problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the first half of the year 1992, the relations were correct. We would adopt decisions unanimously.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Was there a significant meeting held in April or about April 1992 regarding the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, a significant statement made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in late April 1992, a very important meeting was held of the crisis staff in Vitez. We wanted to agree upon the take-over of the weapons from the military base in the vicinity. The former Yugoslav People's Army had, prior to that, taken the weapons that belonged to the Territorial Defence in the municipality of Vitez and other municipalities as well, and these weapons were paid for from the public budget. At the end of the meeting, Mr. Anto Valenta said, and this was something that was not on the agenda, that the Muslims in Vitez had to place themselves under the command of the Croatian community Herceg-Bosna because they stood no chance of staying -- remaining in Vitez. During that occasion, he said that the Croats had already armed themselves, that is, the HVO of the Vitez, that 90 per cent of the population was armed and, according to his estimate, he thought that only 10 per cent of Muslims were armed. There was a military unit in Vitez which was called HOS, H-O-S, and he said that they did not represent any kind of force for them in Vitez at the time. The chairman of the crisis staff said, "Anto, you always complicate things. Leave that aside now." He said, "I'm not joking. You should take this seriously." Anyhow, it was the chairman who ended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, how did relations progress between the Bosnian Muslim and the Bosnian Croat communities in Vitez after that particular announcement by Mr. Valenta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't take it seriously and, as far as I could tell, neither did representatives of the Croatian community. We simply went on with our work and we cooperated, we worked together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were there any incidents which came around in about May that indicated things might not be quite so harmonious?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first incident between Croats and Muslims in Vitez took place on the 20th of May. The president called me around quarter past midnight, that was therefore on the 21st of May, and told me that I should urgently come to a meeting of the crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Was that Mr. Santic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I found other members of the crisis staff in his office. They were all there, together with Santic. At the meeting of the crisis staff was Mario Cerkez, he was the commander of the HVO in Vitez, and he was under the influence of alcohol. Mr. Ivan Santic then stated the reason why we were being called to that meeting, and he said that an incident had occurred in the local hotel and that one young man, young Muslim, was killed, a member of the Territorial Defence. He said that two men were arrested. Then Mario Cerkez said that these three young men had come to the cafe of the Vitez Hotel, that they were provoking those who were present there, and as they were going out of the hotel, the HVO guard apparently shot at one of them and killed him, and the two others were subsequently arrested. The conclusion at the meeting was that we should have an investigation into the incident, that the family would be told about the killing of that young man, and that these two arrested Territorial Defence members should be released. They were wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: This is the first -- sorry to interrupt you, Doctor, but that was the first incident, was it, of violence of that type?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could I just advance you from there to, in fact, the middle of June? If we look to the date of the 18th of June, was there any significant event in the area at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the 18th of June, sometime in the afternoon, HVO formations took over the building of the local police, the town hall, and the building where the Vitez Territorial Defence used to be located. They disarmed the civilian policemen there who were all of Muslim nationality, and they raised the flag of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna and that of the Croatian State.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What was the response to that by yourselves on the crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time -- well, we simply wanted to know why that was happening. Ivan Santic was not in Vitez at the time. We were looking for him because we wanted to know what this was all about because we didn't have a clue, the Commander of the Territorial Defence headquarters didn't know what was going on, the President of the Assembly didn't know either. All we could see at the time were HVO soldiers in uniform in hamlets, in the street, and also around the buildings that I just mentioned. As far as I remember, it was a weekend, and after he returned to Vitez, Ivica Santic convened a meeting of the crisis staff. During that meeting, the chief of the Vitez MUP, Pero Skopljak, stated that the Croatian people were losing patience and that they wanted to take things into their hands. Anto Valenta, as President of the Vitez HDZ, said that this had been done by a group of irresponsible individuals who were not under their control. At the same meeting, they requested representatives of the Bosniak ethnic community, the Muslim ethnic community, to place themselves under the command of the -- to place the Territorial Defence under their command -- at that time, the Territorial Defence was already called BiH army -- that the civilian police should also be placed under their command, and that the officials who were working at the town hall should take up their posts in the newly established one-nation government, the government that was actually the HVO of Vitez. The representatives of the Muslim population refused that. They deemed it to be an attack to the legally elected authorities, those who were elected in November 1990, and they thought it was an attack on the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they refused to become part of that government. We thought that it was a coup.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: After that, how were relations between the communities, say between June and October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That newly established government, the Vitez HVO, set up control points at the entrance to the town of Vitez, controlling every possible movement into and out of the town, including passengers, goods, private cars, trucks, and so on. They adopted a series of new taxes. They had taken over complete control of the life in Vitez, including public enterprises, and all resources ended up in the hands of the new government. As for the representatives of the Muslim population, they were again asked to take part in the new government, but it was all done with numerous threats. They wanted everybody to sign a new organisational scheme of the government, and they said that whoever fails to do that would lose his or her job.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What about the effects actually on the streets for civilians? Were people still moving freely around the town and not molested by anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the very beginning, after the new government had been established, mistreatment and harassment only took place at the checkpoints, that is, at the entrance to the town. However, later on, this became common in the residential parts of the town of Vitez as well, especially in areas where the population was mixed. At one of these meetings, Mr. Pero Skopljak, the then chief of the Vitez MUP, stated that the Serb population of the town of Vitez was placed under the protection of the HVO. On that occasion he stated, and he actually showed us a list to the effect that the residents of the village of Tolovici near Vitez had surrendered to the HVO 120 automatic rifles, two recoilless guns, and a large amount of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If I just may move off that for a moment to an organisational matter? Did the Muslim community respond with any particular organisation of its own? Did you set up any kind of body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We convened a meeting of the representatives of all political parties in the area, but only Muslim representatives and prominent citizens of Muslim nationality, and we presented them the attitude of the executive council of the SDA regarding the formation of the HVO government in Vitez. On that occasion, I think that this happened on the 10th or 12th of July, a coordination board for the protection of Muslims in Vitez was established, and it consisted of 19 members, representatives of all parties, prominent businessmen, and representatives of the local commune. We adopted a declaration on that occasion stating conclusions of that meeting. That declaration stated that the Muslims in Vitez did not recognise the newly established one-nation government in Vitez, that is, the HVO government, and that all decisions adopted by that government would not be binding to Muslims. An order, an instruction was issued to all officials who were holding important positions, they were supposed to continue working on their functions, but in accordance with the results of the elections that took place in November of the previous year, in 1990, and we stated that the Muslim population would recognise only those instructions and decisions that were adopted in accordance with the law. Also, that the Muslims in Vitez would honour all the decisions adopted by the presidency of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
