utterances.text: In a practical sense, Doctor, as we go from June through towards October of 1992, what actually occurred within Vitez? What happened in particular to certain Muslim-owned businesses or shops or other property within the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The period between July 1990 and August, during that period, a number of checkpoints were established, so there was a lot of harassment in that period; and only later on, at the beginning of November 1990, did a series of incidents of blowing up privately owned premises started occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, could I just interrupt you a moment about the date? I think you said 1990. Are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1992. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. You said there were certain things that happened to property. Would you please describe briefly what that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vitez, at the beginning of that period, the first incident took place after -- the second incident happened on the 20th of October in Vitez after a killing incident which happened somewhat earlier. At that time, it was an open conflict in Vitez. Conflicts between the HVO and the BiH army in Novi Travnik happened. Members of the Territorial Defence set up an obstacle; they wouldn't let the HVO soldiers from Busovaca, Kiseljak, and Kresevo -- they prevented them from going to Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And about how far -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And, as I said, an open conflict occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you say there was an open conflict between the BiH forces and the forces of the HVO. That was in Novi Travnik and in Vitez, you were saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, go around the weekend of the 17th or 18th of October to Travnik itself to work in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, I had my regular job in Vitez, but I also worked part time in Novi Travnik -- Travnik, and I worked at the internal medicine ward in the Travnik hospital at that time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And over that weekend, did the patients who came in, did they include military people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I myself did not admit any patients while I worked there; however, when I handed over my duty, my shift, and when I went to Vitez to continue working there, I saw a number of injured, wounded people that were being brought in an ambulance to the surgery department in Vitez, and I wanted to know who these people were, and I was told that they had come from Novi Travnik and that there had been a conflict between the HVO and the BiH army in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I see. So you arrived back in Vitez. Did you hear anything else relating to any kind of armed incidents within the area, any conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I completed part of my duty there. At that time, I was head of the medical centre in Vitez. I was very tired and I went home to get some sleep. As for the conflict in Vitez, I learned about them only on Monday morning -- no, Tuesday morning, sorry, when I went to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you see at work people bearing injuries? You said -- who had been brought into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: In Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, later on, but not at that time, not at the moment I arrived, on that morning. I saw them later on in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What sort of injuries did those people -- or had those people sustained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people who lived in the neighbourhood of Kolonija had mainly sustained gunshot wounds. Most of them were residents of Muslim ethnic background. None of the soldiers, HVO soldiers, was admitted to the hospital on that day. Mostly civilians were coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, you've referred, Doctor, to the 20th of October. Are there any other incidents that are particularly relevant on that date, October '92?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said I also worked as head of the medical centre in Vitez, and I was told by my personnel that on that evening, Marijan Cerkez had been to the medical centre in Vitez, Marijan Cerkez was the HVO commander in Vitez, and Sefkija Dzidic, commander of the Territorial Defence in Vitez, and they told me that they had not reached an agreement and that an open conflict was likely to take place. Sometime during that day, I was asked by a Croat from Vitez, his name is Ilija Safradin, a favour. He told me that his personal car had been requisitioned, and he asked me to do something about that so his car would be returned to him. So together with the driver of the ambulance, Stipo Kristo, I went to the Territorial Defence command in Vitez which was quartered at the secondary school building, and there I found about 15 soldiers, and I told them I wanted to see their commander, and they told me that the building of the command had been shot at during the night and that it was relocated to Stari Vitez. So I went to Stari Vitez in the ambulance, and I found the commander, Sefkija Dzidic, there, and I asked him -- I told him that the car that had been requisitioned from that gentleman should be returned. He did that, that is, he ordered a military policeman to return the keys of the car, but he asked me to get in touch with the commander, Mr. Ivica Santic. He said that by order of the crisis staff in Zenica, an obstacle had been set up on the road to Ahmici. He said that there would be a change in shift of soldiers at the front-line. That was the front-line against the Serbs. And he asked me to try and organise a meeting and calm down the situation in Vitez. I did that. I convened a meeting with the assistance of the then chief of the UNHCR office, Mr. Andersen. Sefkija Dzidic came to the meeting, together with Sulejman Kavazovic, who was chief of the Territorial Defence in Vitez. I was supposed to attend the meeting as well because the politicians were not represented in any way. So when I went to that meeting, I heard gunfire from the direction of Gradina and I asked Ivan Santic for an explanation, and he just said the Muslims are advancing. So I went back to the medical centre, and the headquarters of the Territorial Defence in Vitez were attacked at that time. The HVO soldiers took control of the building, the building that belonged to the logistics in Vitez, they broke into the premises of the SDA in Vitez, they took possession of the documentation that they found there, and later I learned that HVO soldiers demolished and destroyed the Plavac Hotel in Vitez. That hotel was the private property of Hakija Delilovic, and Hakija Delilovic was a local commander of the BiH army in Kruscica near Vitez. So because of these developments, a member of the Territorial Defence was killed in Kruscica, and a number of HVO soldiers were arrested, and I learned for the first time about Mr. Anto Furundzija who was captured at the time. Later on, I had contacts with representatives of the army, and everybody seemed to be very surprised because Anto Furundzija had been one of the commanders of the military police of the Territorial Defence, and he left the Territorial Defence rather late, in September. He took the weapons that he had signed out for, and I think that he was later on released. Prisoners had been taken on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So moving forward from the events of that October, what particular steps did the Muslim community take in regard to their own authorities later in 1992? Did you change the way you governed your affairs or tried to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1992, we still maintained contact with HDZ representatives, in Vitez, and it was as late as November, perhaps in late November, the 25th or 26th of November, the entry into the municipal hall was forbidden to all Muslims who had not signed a statement of loyalty to the HVO government, so that the president of the local government and other officials representing the Muslim side in Vitez were also forbidden entrance. Then I think it was after October, that is, the 20th of October, the civilian police left the building of the joint police and set up a police station in old Vitez. Officials of the Muslim origin then moved and organised their authority in old Vitez. This authority, this government, was rounded off by the decree of the presidency of the republic, the war presidency was elected, and as of the 2nd of February, '93, I became the chairman of the wartime presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When did the, if I can use the expression, Muslim war presidency, when did that, in fact, come into being?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was founded on the 15th of January, 1993, and they prevailed upon me to agree to consent to become its president. I've never been actively involved in politics before that, I was never a politician, I'm not that now, and I tried to evade it. But some others thought that I maintained very good relations with everybody else in Vitez and I would therefore manage to avoid -- to forestall a conflict in Vitez. So I agreed and accepted the nomination on the 2nd of February, '93, although I continued my work as a physician.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could you explain, please, what authorities and what power the war presidency exercised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The war presidency was -- had the supreme authority in the municipality for the civilian protection, for the police, and for the army. It issued orders which had to be put through. Adopted conclusions, issued communications. So it was the highest-ranking authority in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the Muslim population, for the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did the war presidency have any particular executive authority in respect of the army, of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there comes a point where the leading of the witness should stop. The witness was asked a question, he gave an answer, it wasn't enough, and then the Prosecutor is attempting to lead the witness. I would ask that the leading of the witness stop. The questions being asked are of the leading nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Davidson, the particular question you chose was not, in my view, a leading question. It was a general question as to whether the war presidency had any particular executive authority in respect to the army. That seems to me to be an open question and one that is not objectionable. Of course, if counsel starts to lead the witness, we will stop him, but there is no reason for that objection. Mr. Blaxill, I'm sure you will have all that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes indeed, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, have any contact with the military of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The war presidency and myself, as its president, were, of course, the superiors to the army in Vitez. We appointed the commander of the local armed forces of the army and they could do nothing without the authorisation, without the consent, of the war presidency. The same holds true of the civilian police. In other words, we had the authority to appoint the personnel, the executive personnel, and even though the army had regional territorial network and there was the district command of the Territorial Defence of Zenica and the commander on the statistics staff was Merdan Dzemal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So were you aware of the location of the forces of the army of the BiH at about that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And did you keep up any contact with representatives of the HVO during this period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (No answer translated).

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What were the conditions around Vitez, let us move say to the end of January 1993, what were the conditions around Vitez at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conditions, they were impossible. The local population were killed; two eminent Nasaponos (phoen) of Muslim nationality were killed there, Hasan Skopljak and Esad Sajkic. A number of people were beaten, were harassed, their money was taken away, people were brought in for questioning, houses of eminent Muslims were broken and entered, for instance, Suad Salkic's house was broken into in the night hours, they were physically harassed, and ill-treated, around two or three o'clock in the morning, they broke and entered the house of Dzaradzijan Rezvanovic who was a doctor of technical sciences. On the 27th of January, Vitez was under complete blockade by the HVO forces. That is, all the access roads were blocked. They were disarming mostly the members of the army and civilians too, and army members and members of the civilian police, and also mining individual facilities were mined full of Muslims, that is either shops for instance, or whatever facilities or vehicles from Travnik or Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Again, within the town of Vitez, what was it like during the day by comparison to during the night for the citizens living there at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning hours, one could bear it, it was tolerable, but at night, it was really unbearable. Many people complained, complained of those breaking into houses, entrances into houses, harassment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So if I can move forward, what were the conditions pertaining then from the end of January say to the end of March, over that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The situation of -- some contact was established, it was the end of January. In Vitez, understanding was reached between the party for democratic action, SDA, represented by Fuad and Munib Kajmanovic on one hand and Ivan Santic and I think the other one was Dragan Radic, they tried to calm the situation down, and it was suggested that it be addressed at a meeting held by both parties and to set up a war government of Vitez which would not be ethnically coloured. But Mr. Dario Kordic, in a speech transmitted by television, I did not hear it, said literally that all the decrees of the Croat community of Herceg-Bosna needed to be respected or else they would defend it for all their worth. So a contact was established insofar SD armed forces were concerned, that is, the head of the chief of staff of the army of BH, Sefer Halilovic, at the time, and that the chief of staff, Milivoj Metkovic. There was also contact between the commander for western Bosnia and the commander of the third corps. A joint commission was set up made of civilian and military police and they were charged with calming the situation down or bringing the tension down. There was this so-called commission for incidents, for conflict situations, and this commission was supposed to report on the situation in the field regularly and to account to the chief, to the main commission which had its seat at the Tisa Hotel in Busovaca. So the state of affairs improved slightly, but in March and then in April, the disarmament started again. First, the security personnel in special purpose plants in Vitez were requested to lay down their arms, to turn over, rather, their arms, and then they began to disarm the soldiers of the BiH army at a meeting held on the 15th of April of this commission for incidents, for conflict situations. I was told that the Croat representatives were requesting an urgent meeting of the most responsible persons in Vitez because the situation had grown unbearable. And I convened the war presidency and we agreed to a meeting which was to be held on the 16th of April at 12.00, at 1200; however, in the morning of the 16th of April, the HVO in Vitez and other units which were there carried a massive attack, and although --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could I stop you there for a moment, Doctor? I will, indeed, now turn your attention to the date of the 16th of April but, firstly, could you tell me where you were on the day before, the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, I was in the medical centre and I was doing my job. I mean, I was a physician at the time. I was called, I was invited to go to the office of the war presidency in Vitez and I went there. The commission for conflict situation composed of Sefkija Djidic, Sefet Sevro and Niaz Sevro asked me to convene a meeting of the war presidency, and I was told that the Croats were proposed saying a meeting of the most responsible personalities, persons in Vitez from the Croat and the Muslim side and suggesting that a meeting be convened on April the 16th at 12.00. And we agreed with this time and also agreed with the agenda, that is, that all the armed forces be placed under the joint commander, the same would go for the police, and to create a joint command in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you observe anything on the streets of Vitez when you went to go to this meeting? Was there anything particular or unusual you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The meeting was adjourned sometime around 1500 -- no, I should say 1700; that is, 5.00, 1700; and I started to go -- I was on my way home but I did two house visits, no, one house visit, and I also examined two women. One was Mara Bekavac in Rijeka; and another Croat women from Krcevina, I did not examine her, but her husband came to the house of Zvonko Bekavac with another Croat and asked me to help his wife. So I went back home and a number of local people called me at night. In Vitez at night you heard explosions. It was a regular occurrence there at the time, and it was also a normal occurrence for a facility, for a building, to go up in air. What was going on in Vitez, I kept telling everybody that a joint meeting had been scheduled for the 16th of April at noon, at 12.00, and that I expected that we would be able to solve the problems, the pressing problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If I may just stop you at that point, you've made a reference to hearing explosions at night. Had you heard this before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The largest number of them one could hear in November and in January; in other periods, not all that many, but in early November and in January, and then on the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could I just stop you there at that point? Did you ever see the results or affects of what these explosions were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw the business bank in Vitez demolished; also the selling outlet, a number of private stores, private shops, demolished, destroyed around Vitez. I wasn't the only one who saw that. All the inhabitants there, all the locals, could see the result, the upshot of the previous night.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. If we can return now, indeed, to the night of the 15th and the 16th of April, I believe you have said that you spent the night at home in your apartment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So what happened the following morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in my flat with my wife and my three children and my parents-in-law, my wife's parents, who were refugees. At about half past five, we were awakened by detonations, explosions, so we got up to see what it was all about. I called the commander of the Territorial Defence in old Vitez and I asked him, "What is going on?" And he told me that HVO had attacked the BiH army, that it had attacked Vitez, and that in old Vitez there was fighting around houses. And I said, "Man, we're having a meeting today." He said "Nothing doing," he told me. "So what should I do," I asked him, and he told me just to stay put. My next-door neighbour, somebody rang the door, and we looked through. It was my next-door neighbour, Marinko Katava. I and my wife opened the door and he said, "Morning, Neighbour. I've only come to tell you that you are no more, that you are gone. I had already warned you that your children shouldn't shout around the staircase. Long live the army of BiH, and to write graffiti on the walls which you did not heed to this. So just don't get surprised what can happen to you, what will happen to you," and then he went back to his flat which was below ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What did you do after that, Doctor, after that visit? Did you remain at home or did you go out anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I stayed in. I stayed in my flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What, if anything, were you able to observe from your flat in the surroundings outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were terrible explosions. Through the window, I could see shells falling around the houses in the village of Nadioci. In Vitez, I could see smoke rising from the houses inhabited by Vitez Muslims in the town itself, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you see any kind of people actually on the streets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through the window of my apartment, I could see a street, and there were many entrances, four or five, and at each of them there were armed men standing there. I knew them. They were mostly of Croat ethnic origin. Because it was not very far away, I could see them and recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, these armed men, were they wearing any form of uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those, you mean, who were standing in the entrances into buildings? No -- well, some of them, some, here and there, wore a camouflage jacket but they were not wearing full uniforms. They were not in combat gear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Okay. So what happened a little later that morning, say, at about half past eight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A few hours later, that same neighbour who had been there at half past five came around nine or half past nine and wanted to talk to me, tête-à-tête. So we moved to a room where there was no one, to an empty room that was the nursery in my flat, and Marinko Katava, my neighbour, asked me -- the first thing he asked me was what have I done, how have I helped other people so that they saved me, so that they saved my life or spared my life? He also said that he would tell me who had saved my life, but all that fire, all that shooting and everything else and this whole adieu, would calm down by Monday and then he would tell me who it was. He brought me two boxes of cigarettes, two packages of cigarettes. As he was sitting there, another Croat entered, a friend of mine, Dragan Safradin, applied chemist, and he was crying and told me not to be afraid anymore, that the worst was over, to stay in my flat, and also brought me a package of cigarettes, and they left my flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, how long did you, in fact, remain in your apartment before you went out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the apartment, well, I stayed there until Monday. It was April the 19th until 10.00. At that time, a military policeman, an HVO military policeman, or at least that was the kind of uniform he was wearing with the white belt, he came for me or, rather, he asked for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, may I ask you: What, if anything, more had you observed between the 16th and the 19th when the military policeman came to your apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was forbidden for us to leave our apartment, to leave the building or to go to the shelters, so we mostly stayed in the corridor inside the apartment. That was the safest place in the apartment. On the 16th, Stipo Krizanac, another of my neighbours, and Safradin, whose first name I can't remember, went from flat to flat, and there were about 12 flats in our part of the building. And they told -- rather, asked everyone, they wanted to know how many weapons they had, and they told people to surrender weapons or else the HVO policeman would come and search their weapons, and whoever is found in possession of any weapon would be killed. I didn't have any weapons at home, and when he left, my wife told me that a neighbour of ours had brought to our balcony four hand grenades. This neighbour's name was Harun Suljevic. So I didn't know what to do and then my wife went to see Stipo Krizanac, and she took him the hand grenades and she told him that the grenades had been brought that morning by someone else to our balcony and left there. This is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Where did you later then go with Dragan Calic on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question? I'm having problems with these headphones. They keep falling off. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, yes, I was going to say, where did you go with the man you've referred to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, can we have a break at this time --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- for 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. In essence, we have made more progress than I might have anticipated, so I'm more than happy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We shall have a break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we may continue with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. With your leave, Madam President, Your Honours ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, I think we had reached the stage of the 19th of April, 1993, and you had advised the court that a gentleman called Dragan Calic, a policeman, came to your apartment. Can you tell me, please, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 19th of April, Monday, around 10.00, a military policeman of the HVO, whom I knew very well, came to my flat and wanted to see me. My mother-in-law wanted to know what it was all about, but he wanted to see me and I came out and said, "Hello." And then he told me that I should go with him, explaining that he had been sent by one of the local commanders in Vitez, Darko Kraljevic. He said they had a number of wounded soldiers and they needed my help, and he said that I should not be concerned. I took my bag and went with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to a shelter, which was part of the local school for arts and crafts, and these premises had been set up for war emergencies, and as a member of the crisis staff, I participated in the preparations of this particular shelter. It was an outpost of the medical centre in Vitez which was supposed to be used in case of war. When I entered this shelter, the medical staff, who happened to be there, was taken by surprise when they saw me. A nurse stood up and kissed me, and she said, "See? Our doctor is alive." I should explain this. On Saturday, I heard news on TV. According to the news, I had been killed, so that's why they were surprised to see me there. And, indeed, there was a lot of work to do on that day. There were a lot of wounded people coming to the shelter, and they gave me a white coat and all other accessories and I started giving first aid to the wounded people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, could I ask --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the day, most of the people we admitted were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I was going to ask you that very question. Who were the people who had been admitted to the hospital that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The majority of them were HVO soldiers, and occasionally a civilian, a Muslim civilian. On that day, we admitted a number of wounded people from the area of the village of Dubravica and a few from the village of Veceriska. I don't know exactly how many there were, but we had a lot of work that day. We were quite busy. After my arrival in this shelter, maybe one hour later, Mr. Darko Kraljevic arrived, and as I say, I knew him very well, so he said "Hello" to me and he asked me how I was. Then he turned to the medical staff and he told them, "From now on, the head of these premises is Dr. Mujezinovic. You can ask him for whatever you need." And he left two telephone numbers to me and told me that I should call him if necessary. He had his escort with him, all these people were very well-armed, and he was carrying a big knife stuck in his belt. After that, they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you, Doctor, at that time learn of any of the locations of the explosions and so forth you had heard or seen on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Two nurses who lived in the village of Ahmici, one is called Ankica Ljubas, that's her maiden name, she was married to a man called Pujub. That nurse used to work at the internal medicine department in Travnik, and I wanted her to be brought into work with me because she was a very qualified nurse and she was very good. And the other one didn't work at our institution but --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I don't really want to cut you short, but I think the names of the staff probably are not particularly relevant. You say that these members of staff spoke to you. What was it they mentioned to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These two nurses told me that during the night, on the 16th of April, residents of the village of Ahmici, that is, Croat residents of Ahmici, had moved out and went to the Lasva River Valley, and she also said that in the morning, around half past five, a general attack was carried out against the village of Ahmici from three directions, and she said that a number of houses were set on fire in Ahmici, that a lot of children and women were killed, that the cattle was let loose, there was no one to take care of livestock. As they were telling this story, they were both crying. She said that everything that they had seen in Ahmici was sheer horror and that a terrible massacre had taken place in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, we'll just make it clear. Of course, you did not witness any of this yourself, did you? This was just told to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. These two nurses told me what had happened there. I did not see it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, did you continue working at the war hospital after the 19th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked all day long, and around 8.00 p.m., that is after 8.00 p.m., two HVO military policemen arrived, whom I also knew very well, one was Anto Kovac, and the other one was Ratko Nuk, and they told me to come with them, and the medical staff wanted to know where they were taking me, and they simply ordered me to go with them, to follow them. They were armed. They took me to Vitez, to the building of what used to be known as Workers University, to the office which was part of the command of the Vitez brigade. That was the office belonging to the commander of the brigade, Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, of which armed forces the Vitez brigade formed a part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know that they were all HVO members. I believe it was the HVO, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I see. And you say you were taken to an office there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And who did you encounter in that office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that office, I saw Mario Cerkez, Zeljko Sajevic, Zvonimir Cilic, Stipo Zivoja, Dragan Rebac, and Boro Jozic. All these people were known to me very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were they or were they not all military people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, they were all wearing uniform. They were members of the military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And of what armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, they were members of the Vitez brigade of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: All right. Was anything said to you when you were brought in to see these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was addressed by Mario Cerkez, the commander, who asked me, "Doctor, are you aware of the situation you're in?" And I told him I was. And he asked me whether I had heard about Ahmici, and I said I had. And then he said, "Then you know everything." And he told me that I should follow the orders. The others kept silent, and I was just listening to him and he went on. He said that the units of the army had pierced HVO lines in the village of Dubravica and in the area of Zabrdje as well. He told me to call the 3rd Corps, that is, the commander of the 3rd Corps, and to tell them that the HVO in Vitez is holding captive 2.203, I believe, residents, and if they should continue with their advance, that they would kill all the prisoners that they were holding.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, could I ask you at this stage: How far away from Vitez or the places you've mentioned, Dubravica and Zabrdje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the distance between the headquarters and Dubravica, where I was told the line had been pierced, is, I believe, maybe two and a half, three kilometres. As for Zabrdje, it is a summer resort, a mountain resort, and it is somewhat further away from Vitez. I don't know exactly how far it is. There are several roads leading to Zabrdje, 9 kilometres or maybe 12 kilometres, depending on the road you take.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, you say you received some instructions to make telephone calls, one of which was to the commander of the 3rd Corps. Of what force is that 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 3rd Corps of the BH army which had its headquarters in Zenica. That corps at that time was commanded by a person by the name of Hadzihasanovic. I don't know his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Aside from being told about making telephone calls, were you asked to do anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. When I had done with these telephone calls, Mario Cerkez asked me to appear in the local TV and to address an appeal to Muslims in the old part of Vitez, that is Stari Vitez, and to tell them to surrender their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, make any -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, he also wanted me to appear on the local TV and to ask that the Muslims in Stari Vitez surrender their weapons. After that, he wanted me to set up a team that would negotiate with the representatives of the HVO, and I wanted to know who he had in mind, who should be a member of that team, and then he said, "Doctor, in the basement here there are 300 prisoners who are in the basement of that building," and he told me to go downstairs and to select people from the basement, which I did, under the escort of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you make any of the telephone calls that were requested of you, either before or after you went to the basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was before I went to the basement. I knew the telephone number of Mr. Ramiz Dugalic who was in charge of security of the 3rd Corps of the BH army. He's from Vitez. So I called him, and I told him what Mario Cerkez wanted me to do, that he would kill all prisoners and that there were 2,200 prisoners and that he would do that if the BiH army didn't stop the advance, so I asked him to give me telephone numbers of his commander, telephone numbers of Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Granic, Mr. Silajdzica, because he had also wanted me to report to them and to tell them what the situation was. Ramiz Dugalic told me to give him the number I was calling him from, and I gave him that number and he said that he would call me back within next half an hour. And he indeed called me back, and he said that whatever Mario Cerkez was asking for should be obliged, that I should do as he said, and that the advance of the BH army would be stopped. The commander Hadzihasanovic called me as well and also Ejub Ganic who at the time was a member of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So after these discussions, I went downstairs to the basement of the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And what did you see when you went down to the basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I got there, I saw a huge number of people, all of whom were Muslims, residents of the town of Vitez. Among them there was a number of professors, teachers, a lot of retired people, quite a few ill people, disabled people, and I knew most of them, so I went through that area, and I picked up -- I mean, I didn't really pick up anyone, but I just told Bahtija Sivro, Fuad Kaknjo, who was president of the government, Mulahalilovic, director of the high school, Kadir Dzidic who was a professor at the secondary school, to come with me. I think that Zijad Puric also came with us, and we all went together with military policemen, and the owner of these premises, Muazer Gerim, we went to his business premises which were located within the same building. Zvonko Cilic remained with us and so did Boro Jozic. They wanted others to be there as well, and they wanted these people too to make telephone calls and to tell what kind of situation they were in and what was in store for all these prisoners in case the Bosnian army entered Vitez. After a while, I left the office together with Zvonko Cilic, and at about one o'clock I appeared on the local TV as per instructions or, rather, orders of Mr. Cerkez. And I gave a statement. I made an appeal to both sides to the effect that they should stop firing, that they were doing a stupid thing which could only benefit Milosevic, and after that I went back to the office and we stayed there until two o'clock, that is 2.00 a.m., and at that time Zvonko Cilic and Boro Jozic told us that they were threw with us, and if these people had no one else to call, we were advised to remain in the office or we could also go back to the basement. As far as I can remember, it was only Fuad Kaknjo who went back to the basement and we remained in the office of Muazer Gerim. Every 30 minutes a military policeman would come to check on us. Zvonko Cilic and Boro Jozic also told us that Ivica Santic would come the next morning, around 6.00, accompanied by Pero Skopljak, and that they would continue talking with us. They turned up at 5.00 a.m., indeed, and they discussed the situation with us. We were first addressed by Ivica Santic who said that he was sorry that such a thing had happened, he said that there was a number of wounded and killed, but that it was not their fault, that Alija Izetbegovic was to blame, who at the time was the president of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he said that his policy was unrealistic, unreasonable, he said that he wanted to have unitary Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he stated that Bosnia and Herzegovina had fallen apart a long time ago, and he also said that those who were stronger would have the power in Vitez, and he reiterated his threats as well as Pero Skopljak who said something to the following effect -- I mean, I cannot really quote him, but he said that on a number of occasions, he had drawn the attention of the Muslim leaders to the fact that Alija Izetbegovic was leading -- was not working to the advantage of the Bosnian people, and if we did not accept the existence of Herceg-Bosna, that there would be a lot of fighting, and I believe that one of us, and I no longer remember who it was, but I remember that someone said or, rather, suggested that me, as a member of the war presidency, should issue a public statement, that we should explain to the people what the situation was. And I was given a text which had been previously typed out, it consisted of five points, and I signed that paper, which was also signed by Santic. This text was read out for the next five days several times on the local TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, sorry to interrupt you, but at that point you concluded these dealings with these people, had you? What happened on the following day? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military police took me to work and the others went into the basement. The next day, they almost stopped, I mean, the fire stopped, and I went to the premises where the medical centre was. I was dead tired and I laid down on a bed, on a cot where we usually had wounded and I managed to get some sleep. Nobody bothered me that day. That day and the next day, we had nothing. I had no contact with anyone on the Bosniak side, but we heard that the head of the chief of staff of the BiH army had arrived in Vitez, and the commander or the head of the staff of the HVO, that is, Mr. Sefer Halilovic, Milivoj Petkovic, and that the negotiations were underway.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What sort of patients, if any, were being admitted to your hospital at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already said, the first day, there were HVO soldiers and wounded Muslim civilians. Then as the time went by, that is, towards the end of the week, they began to bring in -- first, it was the nurse, Ifeta Dzulabic, that there were women raped and that they needed help.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If I may just turn back for a moment to the soldiers, you say, who had been admitted. Were there any soldiers admitted after that first day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said there were soldiers on the first day. On the second day, they were simply lying there. But the next day, I told you, no, there wasn't much work to do on the second day and there were other physicians around.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, you saw, you said, a number of these soldiers being from the HVO forces --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. He has got his answer to the question. He has posed it now twice to the witness. The witness has answered with respect to his recollection of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So I would ask that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Blaxill is building up another question. Can we hear the question first?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: The second half was going to be: Were you able to identify any particular units from their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, people who came there wore camouflage uniforms, army uniforms, and I really never paid any attention to any insignia, to any markings. They were HVO members, not mostly, but all of them. But which particular unit of the HVO, I really never even looked for it and never had any time for that. If they stayed there on our premises and were hospitalised, they took off those uniforms. As for the wounded, we send them on to Travnik and Zenica by car, and some even to Split. I mean, those who had more severe injuries we were sending on because we simply did not have an operation theatre. Only those lightly wounded were kept in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I see. Did you, in fact, receive any visits from other soldiers, not as patients, but did any military people visit the hospital at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were soldiers who came to see, to visit. But those they knew, they came, they entered with arms; I could not stop them. One day, they told me that Anto Furundzija wanted to see me, and I came out of the building in front of the building and the gentleman --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can I stop you at that point for a moment, please, and just say, you say "they" spoke to you. Can you recall what those people were wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not "they." I said they all had camouflage uniforms with HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, please carry on then, Doctor. I'm sorry I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I came out. Mr. Anto Furundzija was standing there. I used to know him a little, not particularly well because I never had any -- I've never met him before. All I knew was that he was one of the commanders of the military police of the Territorial Defence. And then he asked me, "Doctor, give me the keys to your car." And I said that my car had been stolen and, indeed, it had been stolen, and I had reported it both to the military police of the HVO and the civilian police and the military police of the BiH army, and that I did not have any keys of my car. And he said, "Doctor, I know where your garage is and I'm going there to check it personally. And if I see the car there, I'll come back and kill you myself."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, what was the man you referred to as Furundzija --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I simply did not have a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, what was the person named Mr. Furundzija wearing when he was speaking to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was wearing a uniform with weapons, a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you describe that uniform a little more precisely? Do you recall its colour or any attachments or anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember -- all I can remember is that it was a camouflage uniform, a military camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Was he armed at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and other men with him were armed too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: How close to him were you when you were speaking to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About that (indicating). He came to me and he wanted to ask -- I did not really pay any attention. I mean, he had weapons on him. He was in a uniform and I was afraid. I mean, he couldn't have been more than 50 centimetres away. I mean, he was talking to me directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What were the lighting conditions at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Daylight.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Would you, in fact, have recognised Mr. Furundzija again if you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I invite, Your Honours -- do you, in fact, see anyone of that description here today? If so, would you point in the room and state what the person is wearing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he wears a suit like me. (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You are, therefore, pointing to the person you know as whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anto Furundzija.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, may it please the court that the record could reflect that there was a visual identification and description by the witness of Mr. Anto Furundzija, the accused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: After that, did you continue working in that hospital for a period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I worked there until the 19th of May, 1993. At that time, I was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You have made reference to women being brought in and complaints of rape. Did you personally examine any of these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had agreed with the director of the medical centres, Zvonko Kajic, when we were drawn attention to those women who had been raped, and there were female doctors, female physicians, so we had agreed that those female doctors would take over and examine those women. I did not examine them personally (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I would ask that you not mention any names of these particular people, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If any names mentioned so far could be redacted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were you made aware of where these particular patients came from? Where had they been brought from; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew some of them personally, some I didn't. A woman of a more advanced age, yes, I did notice because she was an older woman, a peasant woman. Somebody said that she came from Tjentiste and she was a refugee in the village of Novaci. My colleagues told me that she had been raped and that she was bleeding from the vagina and anus. After that, that woman had nothing feminine about her, if I may say so. I mean, she was an old woman. Somebody said she was 57. An HVO member, I came out, I think, Stipan Ramiljak, I knew him from the village of Poculica, was standing across the passage and said, "Doctor, see what is ill with your Muslim woman. That's what lies in store for all of you." And I went back into the room. As far as I know, at that time, some five or six women came to us, and I must repeat I did not examine any of them. It was simply agreed that if the injuries were of a grave nature, of a severe nature, that they should be sent to the hospital in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And were these people brought in, essentially, at the same time and in a similar manner to those who had been injured in the combat, the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We used a car that was available to us, so it is possible that they were transported by that same car, I don't know, and I do not know what our lady doctors did with them. We had very few cars at our disposal, so most of the people were simply transported together. I mean, the wounded soldiers and some civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I would like to move on to another factor. You were still, were you, officially a member of the war presidency or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Officially, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: From that day, say, the 19th of April, did you perform any official duties as a member of the war presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: From the date of the 19th of April, did you perform any active duties as a member of the war presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you have any contacts during that period with the military forces of either side, other than the one you have mentioned to us, Mr. Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, except with the wounded. Until about, must have been, Friday, May 16th, 17th, 1993, we had no contact, either with authorised representatives of Croats, apart from what I have mentioned, and twice I was taken by car to Busovaca, again, to treat the wounded and examine civilians. So I went to Busovaca, it was on Tuesdays and Thursdays. We took the military ambulance. They would take me there and bring me back. For awhile, Dr. Muristrako came with me but then he left Vitez, I don't know how, and then after that I went by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And so what was the work you actually carried out down in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Muristrako was with me. He is a surgeon, you know, so we treated the wounds. He treated those wounds and I simply examined various patients. And then after that, I had to do what he used to do, what he used to do before, because in Busovaca, there were no other people who could do it. I mean, there were no medical people there. So at first, I worked in the kindergarten in Busovaca. By the hospital I was accommodated until the outbreak of war, and from there they took me to the medical centre, to the health centre there, to examine civilians. Among those civilians, there were some Muslims. There were some who had been sent to dig trenches and who then complained of back pain, of calluses and things. I simply gave my opinion. I don't know whether anyone heeded to it. All I could do was give advice as to the treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, did you treat very many people on those visits to Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I treated -- I did only control examinations of those with light wounds. All those with severe wounds were being sent to Nova Bila or to Travnik, but those with the most serious injuries, serious wounds, were sent on to Croatia. As far as I could hear from a man who was with the health ministry of Croatia, some of them were transported to Split and some of the wounded Croats were sent on to the hospital in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And what kind of wounds did these people have and could you indicate the causes of those wounds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were injuries from firearms, mostly from firearms. Some of them had been shot in their chest, stomach, head. Some had lost parts of their bodies. I mean, there were different kinds of injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What about the injuries to civilians whom you treated; what were the causes of those injuries by your diagnosis as a doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have any civilians. Nobody ever told me that -- no, with the exception of one civilian brought to me who was a member of the Territorial Defence, and I had seen him in the basement in Vitez. His name was Kousevic, I believe. He was the only one who came to me to tell me that he had been battered by HVO soldiers and broken his jaw. He was the only one who had an injury which must have been inflicted by some blunt instrument or something. The others were other patients. I think his name was Sarif Kousevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Did you, in the time you were in the war presidency, understand in any way the general numbers and the structure of the respective forces in the region? Did you know how many BiH soldiers were in the region or how many HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As the chairman of the war presidency, I knew -- I was informed about the forces, about the numbers, equipment armaments of the BiH army. As for the deployment, the chain of command in the HVO and all the rest, it would be guesswork. I simply didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That's fine. Again, what about, can I just ask you in case I've missed it, the numbers in the BiH forces in the region; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, you see, the soldiers in the army of BiH from Vitez took shifts on the front. And as the chairman of this war presidency, all the rest of us, we never thought we had a front-line there and that there would be a conflict there. There were even strict orders to abstain, to prevent any conflict with HVO because, on one hand, we had a terrible war. I remember an occasion when the president -- when the prime minister of Vitez called Alija Izetbegovic and complained to him about a difficult situation, and he then told us that he had been told by Mr. Izetbegovic, "You may not provoke the Croats. You may not do anything except in self-defence. Only if you are bodily threatened, then you may defend yourselves." As the chairman of the war presidency, I had, evidently, to tell everybody to avoid conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor, I think we are drifting a little from the question that I initially put regarding the overall numbers of the BiH in the region. Can I ask you this question instead: You've mentioned front-lines. Can you indicate generally where any front-lines may have been around the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the 16th of April, because the lines between HVO, I think, were re-established sometime on the 17th or 18th of April, '93, and throughout '93, those lines shifted very little. I could show it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, that has been tendered. I wonder if that map could be tendered to Dr. Mujezinovic and perhaps he could give an indication. I believe we do have a pointer available somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, it can be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If you please, Your Honour, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would have one objection and that would be as to foundation. What is his knowledge of the front-lines based on -- he says he was in his apartment for three days on those dates. If he could lay some foundation as to how he obtained knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: He was the president of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Through what sources did he obtain this information?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm more than happy to ask those.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Before you say anything on this subject, Dr. Mujezinovic, what were the sources of your information? In other words, how did you find this out so that you feel that you know where these places were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learned it on the 19th of May when I left Vitez, when I was exchanged. Those are the lines that I can show. But as regards April and the former half of May, I could not do that, because as a physician, I had to be there. I mean, I was the chairman of the war presidency. They had determined where the lines were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, let me ask you this: Only speak, obviously, to the date where you feel you have that knowledge. But the second thing is: Who, in fact, supplied that knowledge to you? How did you learn this as such? From whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, again, I'm sorry, but we would have an objection. If his knowledge starts from May 19th, we would object as to relevance then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I think I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe his testimony is: "... May, when I left Vitez, when I was exchanged, those are the lines that I can show. But as regards April and the former half of May, I could not do that because, as a physician, I had to be there." So if his testimony is going to be that he can place the lines after he was exchanged, which he has already established is May 19th, we would object as to relevance because it has no relevance then to the situation in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Blaxill? That is a valid point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honour, the point I would make is this, that the relevance, the Prosecution say, is that the existence still of an armed conflict in the region by the 19th of May encompasses the time span of the charge, of the 15th of May. It is not of relevance, particularly, where those lines were on the 15th of May, but it is relevant that the establishment of front-lines and the continued existence of front-lines are indicators of an ongoing armed conflict. That is the thrust of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, again, just from an evidentiary standpoint, he can't vouch that the front-lines that he can draw on May 19th and beyond were established prior to May 19th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no, because the witness has already said he can only say as to what he saw after being exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct. That's our point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: His pointing to any map situation will be limited only to that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't see what the relevance is, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will allow the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I am obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Then, Dr. Mujezinovic, would you please indicate on the map -- if we could have the machine, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may -- I'll only indicate the -- for Vitez, that is, the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you ask the witness to speak into the microphone, please? We cannot hear him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The demarcation lines were Gola Kosa, up here -- or, rather, Kubir, we call it Gola Kosa, Kratine, Banovac, Sivrino Selo, then Tolovici, Grabak; then lies beneath Bukve, Kosovo, then Sadovaca -- between Sadovaca and the village of Zabilje. And then on the other side, Gornja Veceriska, village of Gacice, between the villages Kruscica and Rijeka, the village of Podvranjska. Then here, I think, Crveno Brdce, Vranjska, Rovna, and down here is the municipality of Busovaca. Here, I don't know. I don't know where the lines spread here. So on one bank of the Lasva, I have shown you above Gornja Veceriska, the village of Gacice, the village of Gruscice and Rijeka -- through the village, rather, the line went through the village, and above the village of Vranjska and Rijeka, here on a hill here, I think it was called Crveno Brdce. On the other side, the line went from Kratine to Banovac, beneath the Sivrino Selo, Dubravica, below Tolovici, Grabak. This here is Hrasnica, and the village of Sadovaca. That is as far as I know. And in Vitez, there was a square kilometre -- older Vitez, it was surrounded, it was besieged for ten months. In Vitez, was the front-line of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Your Honours, I am mindful of your announcement earlier regarding timing, and it is now five after five, so I wonder -- it could be a point at which, rather than move to a fresh subject, you might wish to adjourn. Obviously, we're in your hands, Ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You still have more questions in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I have one further area. Yes, indeed, I DO have some. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, I think we will adjourn and then you can continue tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Most obliged, Ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So the court will adjourn and continue tomorrow morning at 9.30 hours

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: 5.05 p.m., to the reconvened on Tuesday, the 9th day of June, 1998, at 9.30 a.m. 25
